===== Protection =====

Protection is an enchantment applied to armor that adds bonus damage reduction.


== Obtaining ==
Protection can be obtained from enchanting tables, drops from mobs that have spawned in a raid,‌[Bedrock Edition  only] books obtained by fishing, monster room chests, librarian villagers, on armor dropped by various mobs, and non-village structure loot.


== Usage ==
Protection reduces the damage taken from all sources except for damage caused by hunger, a warden's sonic boom attack, the void or the /kill command.  This enchantment is capable of reducing damage from sources that normally ignore the user's armor value, such as falling or magic damage from status effects.
The formula for damage reduction is level × 4%, up to a maximum 16% reduction on a single item with Protection IV. If all items are enchanted with Protection IV this gives 64% general damage reduction. The protection enchantment is applied after the armor's damage reduction. The upper limit for damage reduction is capped at 80% (see armor enchantments). It can only be achieved for specific damage types with Fire Protection, Feather Falling, Blast Protection, and Projectile Protection, as each specific damage reduction is twice as effective as Protection.
You can achieve 80% with:
3 × Protection IV + 1 Specific Protection IV, giving you 48% general protection + 80% specific protection
2 × Protection IV + 2 Specific Protection IV, giving you 32% general protection + 80% specific protection
1 × Protection IV + 2 Specific Protection IV + Another Specific Protection IV, giving you 16% general protection + 80% specific protection + 48% another specific protection.
The specific armor piece that Protection is applied to does not influence its strength. For example, applying it to leggings does not cause the player's legs to be more protected than the rest of their body.
Unlike the Blast Protection and Fire Protection enchantments, Protection offers no side effects outside of damage reduction. If applied on wearable items that can't get the enchantment normally, such as a pair of elytra (using commands or an anvil in Creative mode), the enchantment works as usual.


== Incompatibilities ==
Protection, Blast Protection, Fire Protection, and Projectile Protection are mutually exclusive. Attempting to combine these enchantments with an anvil deletes the enchantment in the upgrade slot and replaces it with the enchantment in the sacrifice slot. However, if commands are used to force two or more of these enchantments on the same item, the effects stack. But when the total of the enchantment protection factor provided by the protection enchantments surpasses 20, the rest of these enchantments will no longer directly reduce the damage.

===== Punch =====

Punch is an enchantment applied to bows that increases arrow knockback.


== Obtaining ==
Punch can be obtained from enchanting tables, drops from mobs that have spawned in a raid,‌[Bedrock Edition  only] books obtained by fishing, monster room chests, librarian villagers, and non-village structure loot.
Punch I bows can be obtained by trading with an expert Fletcher.
Skeletons may spawn with a Punch I bow on Normal or Hard difficulty.


== Usage ==
Punch increases horizontal projectile knockback by 3.507 blocks for the first level, then by 3.3 blocks for each subsequent level. The base knockback of projectiles without the enchantment is 1.985 blocks, causing a Punch II projectile to deal 8.792 blocks of knockback.​[more information needed] Punch also increases vertical projectile knockback from 0.8125 blocks to 1.25 blocks, regardless of the level of enchantment.
If a Punch II arrow is blocked by a shield, the knockback effect doesn't apply. By use of commands to increase the level of enchantment beyond II, the enchantment's effect caps at level 255.


=== Specific cases ===
If Punch is applied to a crossbow by use of commands or an anvil in Creative, the enchantment functions when firing arrows but not when firing firework rockets. If Punch is applied to a trident by use of commands or an anvil in Creative, the enchantment does not function.

===== Respiration =====

Respiration is an enchantment applied to helmets that extends how long it is possible to stay underwater without drowning.


== Obtaining ==
Respiration can be obtained from enchanting tables, drops from mobs that have spawned in a raid,‌[Bedrock Edition  only] books obtained by fishing, monster room chests, librarian villagers (or if the "Villager Trade Rebalance" experimental datapack is enabled, a swamp librarian), and non-village structure loot.


== Usage ==
Respiration increases the oxygen bonus attribute (which is 0 by default) by 1 per enchantment level. Every tick, while underwater, the air supply of a player or mob that can drown in water decreases by 1. Wearing a helmet enchanted with Respiration gives a chance for the air supply to not be decreased. The aforementioned chance depends on the enchantment's level, as seen in the following formula: 1 - (1 / (level + 1)). As such, to fully deplete a player's air supply it takes 16 seconds without the Respiration enchantment, 32 seconds (on average) with Respiration I, 48 seconds (on average) with Respiration II, and 64 seconds (on average) with Respiration III. Wearing a turtle shell extends this time by an additional 10 seconds due to the Water Breathing effect.
Since the air supply is increased by 20 every time drowning damage is dealt, the Respiration enchantment also allows to take less drowning damage over the same time period.
Respiration can be applied to non-helmet items by the use of commands.

=== ID ===
Java Edition:

Bedrock Edition:


=== Enchantment definition ===



== History ==


=== Java Edition ===


=== Bedrock Edition ===

===== Riptide =====

Riptide is an enchantment applied to tridents that causes the trident to launch the user when used in water or rain, replacing the trident's ability to be thrown as a projectile.


== Obtaining ==
Riptide can be obtained from enchanting tables, drops from mobs that have spawned in a raid,‌[Bedrock Edition  only] books obtained by fishing, monster room chests, vaults, librarian villagers, and non-village structure loot.


== Usage ==

Tridents enchanted with Riptide can be thrown only when a player stands in water or when exposed to rain. In these situations, a thrown trident launches the player with it. Players can reach greater heights by throwing a Riptide trident straight upward, and travel further distances by throwing it from a higher altitude, or by sprinting or sprint-swimming while in motion. If a Riptide-enchanted trident is held in both the main and off-hands, the player's velocity is not doubled and only the trident in the main is used (see dual wield), although the animation for both tridents is displayed on the HUD. Throwing a Riptide trident consumes 1 durability.‌[JE  only]
The formula for the number of blocks the trident throws the user is (6 × level) + 3 when in rain or standing in water, and (4 × level) + 3 while underwater.
Riptide cannot be used in biomes (or altitudes) where it doesn't rain (unless you are in water), even if the current weather in these locations is snow or overcast.
If the player collides with a mob or another player, the trident deals throwing damage (including critical damage if the player is falling) and the player's movement is abruptly stopped. In this situation, a Riptide trident can bypass the defense of a shield. Colliding with a mob to deal damage consumes 1 durability regardless of version, which means a collision in Java Edition damages the trident twice. If the Riptide trident is in the off-hand, any damage would be dealt with the item in the main hand.
If an item is being held in the off-hand during movement, on the HUD, the held item appears at the top-left, with the top of the item texture facing the direction the player is (unless that item is another trident, in which case the same animation as the Riptide trident is played, regardless of if the trident in the off-hand is enchanted with Riptide or not). The same is true if the trident is in the off-hand and the held item in the main hand, if any. The trident, the item in the main/off-hand (if any), and other items can be swapped, rearranged, or thrown out to create different animation combinations.

A thrown Riptide-enchanted trident can hit multiple targets.‌[BE  only]


=== Elytra ===
A Riptide trident can be used to propel a player wearing elytra if in rainy weather or in a body of water. This allows players to reach speeds upward of 500 blocks per second, compared to 33.5 blocks per second using firework rockets.


== Incompatibilities ==
The Loyalty enchantment cannot be combined with Riptide, as a Riptide trident never leaves the player's hand when used. Channeling is also mutually exclusive with Riptide, both because the trident never lands anywhere, and because it would strike lightning at the player's own position.
If combined using commands, Riptide takes priority over Loyalty and Channeling.

===== Sharpness =====

Sharpness is an enchantment applied to swords, axes, and spears that increases melee damage.


== Obtaining ==
Sharpness can be obtained from enchanting tables, drops from mobs that have spawned in a raid,‌[Bedrock Edition  only] books obtained by fishing, monster room chests, librarian villagers, and non-village structure loot.


=== Enchanting table maximum ===
Certain levels of Sharpness cannot be received directly through the enchanting table on certain equipment tiers, because their enchantability does not meet the required threshold.

The wooden, stone, copper, iron, diamond, and netherite tiers cannot receive Sharpness V through an enchanting table.
The golden tier is the only tier that is able to receive Sharpness V directly through an enchanting table.
Tiers that cannot receive Sharpness V can have it applied to them by use of an anvil, or can be found naturally enchanted with it through certain structure loot.


== Usage ==
In Java Edition, Sharpness adds 1HP extra damage for the first level and 0.5HP × 0.25 for all subsequent levels, using the formula 0.5⋅(level+1).
In Bedrock Edition, Sharpness adds 1HP extra damage for the first three levels, 2HP extra damage for the fourth level, and 1HP extra damage for the fifth level, using the formula ⌊1.25⋅level⌋.
In Java Edition, Sharpness does not apply to charge attacks performed using the spear in the offhand.


=== Damage per hit ===
These tables detail how much damage is done per attack based on the level of enchantment used, assuming the target is not wearing armor and the attack is fully charged‌[Java Edition  only].

==== Bedrock Edition ====

If Sharpness is applied to a bow by use of commands or an anvil in Creative, the enchantment boosts the damage of the weapon's arrows. If Sharpness is applied to a crossbow by use of commands or an anvil in Creative, the enchantment boosts the damage of the weapon's arrows but not its firework rockets.


== Incompatibilities ==
Sharpness is incompatible with Smite, Bane of Arthropods, and Cleaving.​[upcoming: JE Combat Tests] It is also incompatible with Impaling, Density, and Breach; however in Survival these incompatibilities cannot be encountered, as no weapon types have access to both Sharpness and Impaling/Density/Breach. If commands are used to have two or more of these enchantments on the same item, their effects stack.‌[Java Edition  only]

===== Soul Speed =====

Soul Speed is an enchantment applied to boots that causes faster movement on soul sand and soul soil, but slowly drains durability in the process.


== Obtaining ==
Soul Speed is a treasure enchantment. It cannot be obtained from enchanting in an enchanting table. Unlike most other treasure enchantments, it also cannot be obtained from most chest loot (except from chests in bastion remnants), fishing, or trading.


=== Mob loot ===
Piglins may spawn wearing golden boots enchanted with Soul Speed which have a chance to be dropped when they are killed.


=== Generated loot ===
Enchanted books and golden boots with a random level of Soul Speed may appear in bastion remnant "generic" chests.


=== Bartering ===
Soul Speed can be acquired via bartering with piglins, who may offer enchanted books and iron boots with a random level of Soul Speed.


== Usage ==


=== Speed ===
When walking on soul sand or soul soil, Soul Speed multiplies the player's walking speed with 1.3+(0.105⋅level) and removes the slowness from soul sand.
While Soul Speed walkways are not as fast as some other means of transit (such as blue ice tracks), Soul Speed boots do not require vehicles such as minecarts or boats in order to apply their speed boost. This makes Soul Speed walkways useful for increasing movement speed across more uneven or varied terrain where vehicles might prove unwieldy.
Carpets or slabs‌[JE  only] on top of soul sand or soul soil does not prevent the speed increase from Soul Speed.


=== Durability ===
The durability of worn boots enchanted with Soul Speed has a 4% chance to go down for each compatible block stepped on.[verify] This chance can be decreased with the Unbreaking enchantment.


=== Particles ===

Soul particles appear when walking on one of the compatible blocks.


=== General ===
The soul_speed_blocks tag determines which blocks are compatible with Soul Speed.

===== Sweeping Edge =====

Sweeping Edge is an enchantment applied to swords that increases sweep attack damage. This only affects the damage of the sweep attack against other surrounding entities, and does not increase damage against the entity that is attacked directly. Sweeping Edge is not required to do sweep attacks, as swords have the ability innately.​[until: JE Combat Tests]


== Obtaining ==
Sweeping Edge can be obtained from enchanting tables. Enchanted books with Sweeping Edge can be obtained by fishing, from monster room and ocean ruins chests, from librarian villagers, and as non-village structure loot.


== Usage ==
Sweeping Edge increases sweep attack damage by levellevel+1 of the sword base attack damage, meaning level I, II, and III deal 50%, 66.6‾%, or 75% of the sword's attack damage extra. Sweeping Edge is not required to do sweep attacks, as swords have the ability innately. Sweep attacks activate when a player standing on the ground attacks while not sprinting with an attack cooldown at 84.8% or above. The sweep attack damages surrounding entities that are within a 1 by 0.25 by 1 block area of the attacked entity, dealing 1HP and knocking them back. Sweep attacks and Sweeping Edge only affect sorrounding entities and not the attacked one.


== Damage ==
The formula for sweep attack damage is: 1+basedamage⋅levellevel+1+enchantmentdamage HP. Where base damage is the sword's damage before applying enchantments and enchantment damage is the damage added by Sharpness, Smite, and Bane of Arthropods for the target.
For example, an iron sword enchanted only with Sweeping Edge I deals 1+6⋅11+1=4HP damage to each surrounding mob hit with a sweep attack, while a diamond sword enchanted with Sharpness V and Sweeping Edge III would deal 1+7⋅33+1+3=9.25HP × 4.625 damage to surrounding mobs.
Higher levels than Sweeping Edge III (obtainable via the use of commands or third party editors) are processed following the formula above.

===== Swift Sneak =====

Swift Sneak is an enchantment applied to leggings that lessens the movement speed reduction that occurs when sneaking.


== Obtaining ==


=== Generated loot ===
Swift Sneak can be obtained only from loot chests in ancient cities, making it non-renewable. The chests can contain enchanted books with any level of Swift Sneak.


== Usage ==


=== Speed ===
Swift Sneak increases the player's sneaking speed by 15% of their walking speed per level. At Swift Sneak III, the player's sneaking speed equals 75% of their normal walking speed. Swift Sneak IV and V can further increase this, but the sneaking speed can never be greater than the walking speed.
This enchantment also increases the player's movement speed while they are crawling.
It also has an effect in water, but is still slower movement than regularly walking underwater. This holds true even when combined with depth strider, another enchantment upon boots for swimming which further increases underwater walking speed.

===== Thorns =====

Thorns is an armor enchantment that gives a random chance to damage entities that attack the user, at the cost of increasing incurred durability damage.


== Obtaining ==
Thorns can be obtained from enchanting tables, books obtained by fishing, monster room chests, librarian villagers, and non-village structure loot.


=== Enchanting table maximum ===
Thorns III cannot be received directly through the enchanting table on any tier of armor, because their enchantability does not meet the required threshold.
Tiers that cannot receive Thorns III can have it applied to them by use of an anvil, or can be found naturally enchanted with it through certain structure loot.


== Usage ==
While wearing any piece of armor with the Thorns enchantment, each piece independently has a 15%⋅level chance of the wearer inflicting 1HP to 5HP damage (not restricted to integer values) on anyone who attacks them, regardless of whether they were hit by a melee attack, arrow, or other projectile. This damage deals regular knockback to the attacker and regular damage to their armor.
If the player dies as a result of Thorns damage, the death message is "<player> was killed while trying to hurt <entity>".
Multiple worn armor items with the Thorns enchantment stack with each piece offering an independent chance to deal damage to the attacker. However, due to the invulnerability timer, the total damage is capped at the highest individual amount of damage dealt this way. As a result, wearing multiple pieces of high-level Thorns armor pieces increases the overall chance to deal damage and shifts the average amount of damage dealt this way toward the upper end of the possible range, but has a 0 % chance of reaching 5HP and can never exceed it.
Average damage dealt depending on the number of items with Thorns III worn are as follows:

Thorns applies a durability penalty to the armor. It reduces durability by an additional 2 points when inflicting damage. If multiple armor pieces are enchanted with Thorns, the durability penalty is applied to each piece that triggered (even if it didn't end up inflicting the highest damage), regardless of what level of Thorns that piece has. If the item is also enchanted with Unbreaking, the usual probabilities for ignoring each individual point of durability loss apply.
Thorns damage can be blocked by a shield, if there is an opportunity to block, usually because the damage triggering the thorns effect comes from a projectile.
The Thorns effect can trigger from any equipment slot, including e.g. the body slot of horses or holding the enchanted item in the main or off-hand. Although horse armor cannot be enchanted in Survival, in Java Edition the Thorns enchantment can be applied to horse armor in Creative and works when held by the player or equipped to a horse.


=== Guardian thorns ===
Guardians and elder guardians have a Thorns-like effect that inflicts damage when their spikes are out. However, this affects only melee damage, whereas Thorns the enchantment applies to all direct attacks, including ranged.


== Unaffected mobs ==
Wardens using sonic boom attacks are not affected by this enchantment.‌[JE  only]

===== Unbreaking =====

Unbreaking is an enchantment that gives a chance for an item to avoid durability reduction when it is used, effectively increasing the item's durability.


== Obtaining ==
Unbreaking can be obtained from enchanting tables, drops from mobs that have spawned in a raid,‌[Bedrock Edition  only] books obtained by fishing, librarian villagers, and non-village structure loot.


== Usage ==
For tools and weapons, there is a 100%level+1 chance that using the item reduces durability, which means that for levels I, II, and III the item has a 50%, 66.6‾%, or 75% chance of not using any durability. On average, tools last 2, 3, or 4 times as long.

For armor, there is a 60%+40%level+1 chance a use reduces durability, meaning each durability hit against Unbreaking I, II, and III armor has a 20%, 26.6‾%, or 30% chance of being ignored. On average, armor lasts about 1.25, 1.36, or 1.43 times as long. Levels below 0 can lower the chance to reduce durability to less than 60 %.
When durability is reduced by multiple points, for example, when hooking a mob with fishing rods or getting blown up with TNT, Unbreaking is applied for each point of decision of actual reduction.

===== Wind Burst =====

Wind Burst is an enchantment applied to maces that causes a powerful upward knockback effect to be created upon executing a smash attack. Unlike wind charges, Wind Burst does not negate fall damage.


== Obtaining ==


=== Generated loot ===
Wind Burst can only be obtained from ominous vaults in trial chambers in the form of enchanted books at level I. It is a rare enchantment, having a 5.5% chance of being ejected from an ominous vault once activated with an ominous key.


== Usage ==

When performing a smash attack using a mace enchanted with Wind Burst, the user is launched back into the air, allowing them to chain continuous smash attacks. Attacks on the ground do not activate Wind Burst, as the activation requires a smash attack.
In order to perform a smash attack, and in turn activate Wind Burst, a player has to fall more than 1.5 blocks. This can be achieved by jumping off a single block placed on the ground and attacking right before touching the ground (total fall height of ~2 blocks), or alternatively by using a wind charge or the Jump Boost effect.
The slow attack speed of the mace in Java Edition makes it impossible to chain fully-charged smash attacks with Wind Burst I on a target that stays at the same elevation.
Like wind charges, Wind Burst can interact with redstone objects such as levers or wooden doors.
Since foxes can attack mobs by pouncing on them, a fox given a mace enchanted with Wind Burst is capable of activating it. This is of little benefit to the fox, as it will typically fail to chain a second smash attack and will thus take fall damage.


=== Launch power per level ===
Wind Burst adds approximately 8 blocks of upward knockback for the first level, 16 blocks for the second level, and 24 blocks for the third level. In Java Edition, Blast Protection reduces the effect of Wind Burst. In Bedrock Edition netherite armor reduces Wind Burst's effect. The table below details the explosion knockback multiplier and blocks launched per level.

Further Wind Burst levels use the formula 1.15 + 0.35 * level to calculate the knockback multiplier.


=== On other items ===
If Wind Burst is applied to an item other than a mace by use of commands or anvils in Creative mode in Java Edition, Wind Burst activates after the player has fallen at least 1.5 blocks. The launch from Wind Burst doesn't boost the player as high, since landing hits with any other item does not reset vertical velocity unlike the mace. The faster the player falls while hitting an entity, the less it is launched upward, since gravity and the enchantment are close to causing a force equilibrium.

===== Feature =====

Features (also known as generated features) are small decorators generated in each chunk after terrain generation. This page lists generated features in a Minecraft world.

== Generation ==

Features are generated for a given chunk after the terrain has been formed. When features are generated, they can spill over into neighboring chunks that have been previously generated. Thus, a tree at the edge of the generated world may be overwritten by a village before the player reaches it. It is also theoretically possible for two worlds generated with the same seed, from the same version of Minecraft, to differ slightly depending on the players' travel routes, because the chunk generation order may determine which of two conflicting features overwrite or suppress the other.

===== Structure file =====

A structure file (also called structure template) is an NBT file that stores small structures of blocks and entities. Structure files are used to store some structures such as end cities, igloos, and fossils.


== Usage ==


=== Java Edition ===
Structure files are stored as .nbt files in data packs in the  data/<namespace>/structure folder.
They can be saved and loaded using the Structure Block. When saved from Structure Blocks they are saved into the generated/<namespace>/structure subfolder in the world save folder. When no namespace is given, then the minecraft namespace is used.
Structure files can also be placed using the /place template command. They are also used during the generation of some structures and of fossil features.


==== Prebuild structures ====


=== Bedrock Edition ===
Structure files are stored using the NBT format in the game files. In behavior packs, they are stored as .mcstructure files in the structures/<namespace> folder.


==== Prebuild structures ====


== NBT structure ==
All the specified positions are relative to the block located toward  -X, -Y, -Z.

===== Terrain features =====

This page lists terrain features that are created as part of the world generation.


== Overworld ==


=== General terrain generation ===

The surface in the Overworld is generated using 3D Perlin noise, which creates pseudo-random variation. More variation is created by three noise parameters: continentalness, erosion, and peaks and valleys. These are also tied to biome placement.
Some features created by this algorithm include:


==== Hills and lakes ====
Hills in the game can vary from gradual slopes to steep cliffs. They can occur anywhere in the world, including oceans, flatland, or mountains. Hills in an ocean biome can reach high enough to create islands. Similarly, terrain variation can also cause holes and pits, sometimes forming lakes. On an amplified world, hills in most biomes are often extended and form extreme cliffs.
Higher erosion values often result in more "windswept" hills with steep cliffs and generally lower altitudes. At lower erosion, hills are smooth or almost flat, but the terrain can reach much higher elevation.


==== Mountains and valleys ====
When the erosion value reaches lower values, peaks and valleys start to contribute more to the terrain variation. The general altitude depends on the continentalness.
Mountains are high elevation terrain that have jagged peaks and higher land. Mountainous terrain often includes valleys, slopes, cliffs, and peaks. Sometimes, mountains reach the terrain generation limit of Y=256, where they are cut off and form flat plateaus combined with rugged terrain.
In contrast to windswept hills, however, mountains and valleys are smoothly shaped with rolling hills. Plateaus occur at slightly higher erosion or lower continentalness, which are similar to mountains but flattened at around Y=130. More inland, both mountains, valleys, and plateaus can stretch over huge areas with much higher elevation. At the border of different terrain types, steep slopes or cliffs form.
Common terrain features created by peaks and valleys (weirdness) are mountain rings. Mountain peaks or plateaus can enclose lower valleys, although they are sometimes incomplete. When the weirdness reaches extreme values, these valleys can reach extreme depths and form craters, sometimes reaching the bottom bedrock layers. In Bedrock Edition, when this occurs, stone walls more than one hundred blocks tall are formed to separate the water from the lava above the bedrock, creating a sinkhole. Depending on the continentalness, extreme weirdness values can also create huge mountain peaks or surface cave biomes instead.
The peaks and valleys noise usually creates rivers between mountains or plateaus. Depending on the continentalness, these vary in width and depth. High-erosion terrain like swamps can also be affected, but oceans and mushroom fields are not.


==== Cliff ====

Oceanic cliffs are steep vertical slopes that can sometimes generate when mountainous terrain borders an ocean. Oceans near cliffs are often deep and sometimes small. The cliffs expose many caves, while the surface terrain ends abruptly.


==== Fjord ====

Fjords happen when rivers cut through high-medium elevation terrain. Rivers are deeper here than usual.


==== Floating island ====
Floating islands are structures that float in mid-air. Floating islands are normally just small chunks of floating dirt and stone found near cliffs, but on rare occasions they can be large structures that even have springs and trees on them. Floating islands are most frequently found in or near windswept hills biomes and their variants, as well as windswept savannas.
Floating islands and overhangs are common when the erosion is high, but not at its maximum. This results in windswept terrain often surrounding swamps, with flatland terrain nearby.


=== Sea level ===
Air on altitude Y=63 and lower is replaced by water. This occurs mostly in river and ocean biomes – areas in the terrain generation with low continentalness or peaks and valleys – and can form massive, deep water bodies. The sea level can also create lakes in land biomes, or fill deep craters.

Below Y=-55, all air is replaced by lava, forming a similar "lava level". This mostly applies to caves, as the terrain rarely reaches such depths.


=== Surface ===

Based on the depth value calculated by the terrain generation, water exposure, the biome, and the dimension, the world is "filled" with several blocks in layers. The top layer is always defined, and the following layers are determined by a surface depth noise, roughly 5 blocks deep.


==== Terrain ====
All blocks that make up the terrain are placed depending on the dimension and altitude. In the Overworld, this is as follows:

Bedrock: In Java Edition, one full layer at Y=-64, followed by a randomized gradient that places bedrock up to layer Y=-59. In Bedrock Edition, two full layers at Y=-64 and -63, followed by a noise that randomly places bedrock up to Y=-60, meaning that they cannot generate "floating", and the pattern is always the same regardless of world seed. The bedrock layers cannot be overridden by other terrain features.
Deepslate generates up to Y=0. Above, a gradient randomly places decreasing amounts of deepslate up to layer Y=8.
Stone generates anywhere else as terrain block.


==== Surface layers ====
The uppermost layers of the terrain are converted to a biome-dependent material. The first layer is usually grass blocks, the following few layers are dirt. In shallow water, the first and following layers are always dirt, allowing disks to generate. In deeper water, the first layer is gravel and the following layers are stone. A few biomes override this.

 In deserts, beaches, and warm oceans,‌[JE  only] the first few layers are sand. A secondary surface depth generates sandstone, reaching deeper in deserts. Except warm oceans,‌[JE  only] this is not applied in deep water.
 In lukewarm oceans and warm oceans,‌[BE  only] only the first layer in deep water is sand.
 In ice spikes, the first layer above water is snow blocks.
 In mushroom fields, the first layer above water is mycelium.
 In dripstone caves, the first layer above water is stone.
 In mangrove swamps, the first few layers excluding deep water are mud.
 In jagged peaks, the first layer above water is snow blocks and the following layers are stone.
 In Bedrock Edition, in sulfur caves as well as frozen oceans and jagged peaks, below any water, the first few layers are stone.
When gravel or sand generates floating, it gets replaced by stone and sandstone, respectively. The surface layers do not apply to caves, meaning these blocks can still generate floating, and other blocks can be exposed.


==== Special surface layers ====
The following biomes have special surface layers, also known as strips. This is created by 2D noise, making blocks appear in varying patches, blobs, and strips.
 In wooded badlands, above roughly layer 97, coarse dirt and grass blocks alternate as top layer above water.
 In dappled forests, coarse dirt and grass blocks alternate as top layer above water.
 In old growth taigas, coarse dirt, podzol, and grass blocks alternate as top layer above water.
 In stony peaks, calcite and stone alternate as the first few layers, not applied in deep water. This forms long strips across the entire biome.
 In stony shores, gravel and stone alternate similarly, forming strips. Floating gravel is replaced by stone.
 In groves and snowy slopes, powder snow and snow blocks alternate as the first layer, forming patches of powder snow.
In the first layers below, powder snow alternates with dirt in groves or the mountain slopes noise in snowy slopes. This results in powder snow patches reaching depth, while snow blocks cover only the surface.
 In frozen peaks, ice replaces the top few layers in small blobs. Packed ice generates in larger strips between snow blocks, both in the top few layers.
 In windswept hills, as well as frozen oceans in Bedrock Edition, stone replaces most dirt and grass in the first few layers, making the latter generate in patches.
 Similarly, in windswept savannas, stone generates in strips in the first few layers. The top grass layer is replaced by coarse dirt in some patches.
 Windswept gravelly hills use a similar noise to windswept hills but with some gravel alternating in the first few layers. In Bedrock Edition, the noise is different and most of the biome is covered in gravel, with a few one-block strips of grass blocks (or dirt in shallow water).


==== Mountain slopes ====
The jagged peaks, frozen peaks, and snowy slopes biomes all use a mechanism to determine steep slopes. North and east cliffs replace other blocks in the first few layers with stone, or packed ice in frozen peaks, where only a thin snow layer generates on top.


==== Badlands terracotta ====
All badlands biomes have more complex surface algorithms.

Deep water generates as usual in Java Edition with one gravel layer above stone, or entirely stone in Bedrock Edition.
Shallow water replaces the top layer with white terracotta in Java Edition only.
The following above-ground terrain is covered with one red sand layer followed by some orange terracotta layers.
Floating red sand is replaced by red sandstone.‌[JE  only]
Above roughly Y=74, the top-most layer is replaced by terracotta alternating using noise with hoodoo terracotta. The first layers below are always hoodoo terracotta.
Above Y=256, orange terracotta replaces hoodoo terracotta, visible only in amplified worlds.
"Hoodoo terracotta" is generated as follows. Each world seed generates 192 layers of random stained terracotta colors (red, orange, yellow, brown, white, and light gray), corresponding to the Y-coordinates above Y=63. At each horizontal coordinate, each layer may shift up and down by at most 7 blocks based on noise, creating unique variation.


==== Swamp marshland ====
In swamps and mangrove swamps, a noise creates variation near the sea level. At layer Y=63, the surface materials are sometimes replaced by water, which can extend slightly deeper in mangrove swamps. This creates some undeep marshland in the terrain that already alters between shallow water and flat land a lot.


==== Erosion ====

When the surface depth is less than or equal to 0, the top layer is stripped away, exposing the layers below all surface blocks, ususally stone. In badlands, they are made of orange terracotta. Erosions in frozen oceans occur at the freeze layer and replace it with air, followed by ice or water below.
Commonly, minerals can be found in these, generally coal ore and iron ore. Due to a bug, they do not generate in Java Edition.


=== Hoodoo ===
Hoodoos are tall spike-like structures found in badlands at the red sand level. While this structure is found exclusively in eroded badlands, all badlands biomes actually have this structure, but set to false except for eroded badlands. Hoodoos are entirely made up of hoodoo terracotta, making it occur at much lower altitudes, although they can reach more than 100 blocks tall.


=== Iceberg ===

An iceberg is a large terrain feature composed of packed ice and snow blocks.
Large icebergs generate in frozen oceans and deep frozen oceans. They consist of packed ice, and can be topped with snow blocks. Icebergs generate in a wide variety of shapes and sizes, ranging from small islands to giant mountain-like icebergs. They can also generate with cave-like holes (these might be related to the carved recesses in cone icebergs)​[more information needed] in them, which sometimes pass through to the other side of the iceberg.
There are often blue ice features attached to them.


=== Noise cave ===

Noise caves are generated using a noise. They come in the form of cheese caves, spaghetti caves, and noodle caves. By adjusting noise frequency, hollowness (for cheese caves), and thickness (for spaghetti caves, noodle caves, and noise pillars), noise caves can vary in extremely diverse ways. When generating noise caves, the game firstly generates a random noise field, and "smudges" it using a mathematical trick called Perlin noise. These processes then result in a 3D noise image.
Unique features of noise caves are aquifers. Bodies or water or lava may form at different altitudes, separated from other bodies by thin walls or ceilings.
Larger noise caves may feature noise pillars, formations of rock connecting the ceiling with the floor based on noise, which can have varying sizes.

Some noise caves may also reach the surface, exposing stones or creating floating islands.


=== Carvers ===
Carver caves are narrow, winding tunnels similar to noise caves, but with a clear end and a central starting room. They can generate at any altitude and connect to the surface, other caves, or structures. Sometimes, carver caves are filled with water or lava.

Canyons are similar to carver caves, but shaped like a tall ravine and relatively shorter. Canyons may generate entirely underground, underwater, or exposed to the surface, and they can have different sections similar to aquifers. The walls of a canyon are steep cliffs with some edges and natural variation. They can also reach the lava level.


=== Ore veins ===

Unlike ore features, ore veins are terrain features that carve through the world and place several blocks. There are two types: veins with copper ore, granite as filler material, and occasional raw copper blocks, forming in the stone layer, and veins with deepslate iron ore, tuff as filler, and some raw iron blocks, forming in the deepslate layer. Ore veins are massive branching networks, sometimes exposed in a cave, but they cannot replace air or water.


== The Nether ==


=== General terrain generation ===

Terrain in the Nether is generated similarly to the Overworld with 3D Perlin noise. Instead of surface-oriented parameters, the game has two pairs for the solid terrain at the ceiling and ground, and the hollow space in between. This results in cave-like terrain where most air is found in the middle between the ceiling and the ground.
Floating islands, cliffs, and overhangs are common.


=== Lava sea ===
Similar to the water sea level in the Overworld, a lava sea forms below Y=31 in the Nether, which happens quite often. They can stretch for hundreds of blocks in any direction, and are usually bordered by netherrack, or occasionally soul sand, gravel, and magma blocks. Striders can spawn in lava seas.
Unlike with Overworld oceans, lava seas are not handled as a biome. In Bedrock Edition, the lava sea is biome-dependent and can also be generated in the Overworld, replacing the water sea.


=== Surface ===

Based on the depth value calculated by the terrain generation, the biome, and the dimension, the world is "filled" with several blocks in layers.


==== Terrain ====
All blocks that make up the terrain are placed depending on the dimension and altitude. In the Nether, this is as follows:

Bedrock: In Java Edition, one full layer at Y=0, followed by a randomized gradient that places bedrock up to layer Y=5. In Bedrock Edition, two full layers at Y=0 and 1, followed by a noise that randomly places bedrock up to Y=4 meaning that they cannot generate "floating", and the pattern is always the same regardless of world seed. The bedrock layers cannot be overridden by other terrain features.
Bedrock: Another layer of bedrock generates similarly at the Nether roof. This is one full layer at Y=127, followed by a gradient,‌[JE  only] or noise‌[BE  only] that places blocks down to Y=122/‌[JE  only]123.‌[BE  only]
Netherrack generates anywhere else as terrain block.


==== Surface layers ====


==== Nether erosions ====

In the Nether, erosions generate the same size and shape as they do in the Overworld. Unlike their Overworld counterparts, however, Nether erosions replace the ground with netherrack instead of stone. Nether erosions can also expose ores, mainly Nether quartz ore and Nether gold ore.
Notably, erosions generate independent of the y-coordinate; if an erosion generates in an overhang in the Nether, an identical erosion is guaranteed to generate at the exact same x and z coordinates on the ground below such an overhang.


=== Nether carvers ===
Carver caves and canyons generate similarly in the Nether as how they do in the Overworld. Below Y=31, they are filled with lava in Java Edition. In Bedrock Edition, they are filled with air and some biome features, and are separated from the lava sea by walls. They can often expose bedrock, but not at the ceiling.


== The End ==


=== Central island ===
The center of the End is a large, asteroid-like island composed entirely of End stone, floating in the void. It features the exit portal in the center, surrounded by 10 End spikes in a circle. The island is home to the ender dragon, and serves as the arena where it is fought.
At a distance of 1000 blocks away, an endless expanse of additional islands begins, away from the main island. These consist of large islands, about the size of the main island, and smaller ones, which are usually thin and small.


=== Outer islands ===
The outer End islands are found 1000 blocks away from the central island, also made entirely of End stone. They vary in size from large islands to smaller "mini islands". Generated structures such as End cities and End ships spawn here, along with chorus trees and erosions. The player can be taken to the End islands through the End gateway.


=== End erosions ===

Erosions generate in the End as they would in the Overworld and the Nether, but they never expose any ores. End erosions may generate on both the central island and outer islands, and chorus trees can occasionally take root in the erosions.

*** ENGLISH GRAMMAR AND USAGE CORPUS ***

This corpus explains English grammar, punctuation, spelling, vocabulary, and
writing conventions in clear language with examples. It is used for local
language-model training.

===== Why grammar matters =====

Grammar is the set of rules that explains how words are arranged to make
meaningful sentences. A sentence needs a subject and a predicate. The subject
names the person, place, thing, or idea that the sentence is about. The
predicate says something about the subject and must contain a verb.

Example: The cat sleeps. Here "the cat" is the subject and "sleeps" is the
predicate. The verb "sleeps" tells us what the cat does.

Good grammar helps the reader understand the message quickly. It is not only
about following rules. It is about clarity, rhythm, and respect for the reader.
A sentence can be grammatically correct and still be confusing if it is too
long, too vague, or badly organized.

===== The eight parts of speech =====

English words are often grouped into eight parts of speech: noun, pronoun,
verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, and interjection. Many words
can change their part of speech depending on how they are used. The word
"run" can be a verb in "I run every morning" and a noun in "I went for a run."

A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea. Examples: teacher, London,
bicycle, freedom, kindness. Common nouns are general, such as city or book.
Proper nouns name a specific person, place, or organization and are
capitalized, such as Maria, Tokyo, and Minecraft. Concrete nouns name things
you can perceive with your senses, such as apple, music, and wind. Abstract
nouns name ideas or qualities, such as courage, justice, and time.

A pronoun replaces a noun or noun phrase. Examples: I, you, he, she, it, we,
they, me, him, her, us, them, my, your, his, her, its, our, their, mine,
yours, hers, ours, theirs, myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself,
ourselves, themselves. Pronouns must agree with the noun they replace in
number and, in some cases, gender.

A verb expresses an action, an occurrence, or a state of being. Examples: run,
build, think, become, seem, is, are, was, were. Action verbs show physical or
mental action. Linking verbs connect the subject to a word that describes it,
such as "She is happy" or "The soup smells good." Helping verbs, also called
auxiliary verbs, combine with a main verb to form tenses, questions, and
negatives. Examples: do, does, did, have, has, had, be, am, is, are, was,
were, will, would, can, could, may, might, must, shall, should.

An adjective describes or limits a noun or pronoun. Examples: red, tall,
ancient, happy, three, several. Adjectives usually come before the noun, as in
"a red apple," or after a linking verb, as in "the apple is red." Comparative
adjectives compare two things, as in "taller" or "more interesting." Superlative
adjectives compare three or more things, as in "tallest" or "most interesting."

An adverb describes a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. Examples:
quickly, carefully, very, almost, yesterday, here. Adverbs often answer the
questions how, when, where, or to what degree. Many adverbs end in -ly, but not
all do. "Fast" can be an adverb in "He runs fast." "Very" is an adverb in "very
cold."

A preposition shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and another
word in the sentence. Examples: in, on, at, by, with, under, over, between,
through, during, after, before, about, from, to, of, for. A preposition is
usually followed by an object, which can be a noun, pronoun, or noun phrase.
The group is called a prepositional phrase, as in "under the table" or "after
lunch."

A conjunction connects words, phrases, or clauses. Coordinating conjunctions
join equal parts: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. Subordinating conjunctions
join a dependent clause to an independent clause: because, although, if,
when, while, since, unless, until, after, before, though, whereas. Correlative
conjunctions work in pairs: either ... or, neither ... nor, both ... and, not
only ... but also.

An interjection expresses emotion or reaction. Examples: wow, oh, hey, oops,
alas. Interjections are often followed by a comma or an exclamation mark and
are common in conversation and informal writing.

===== Sentence structure =====

A simple sentence contains one independent clause. Example: The dog barked.
A compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses joined by a
coordinating conjunction or a semicolon. Example: The dog barked, and the cat
ran away. A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one
dependent clause. Example: When the door opened, the dog barked. A compound-
complex sentence combines both patterns.

Every complete sentence must have a subject and a finite verb. The subject is
usually a noun phrase. The verb must agree with the subject in number and
person. In commands, the subject "you" is understood and often omitted.
Example: Close the door.

Sentences can be classified by purpose. A declarative sentence makes a
statement. An interrogative sentence asks a question. An imperative sentence
gives a command or request. An exclamatory sentence expresses strong emotion.
The punctuation usually matches the purpose.

A phrase is a group of words that works as a unit but does not contain both a
subject and a finite verb. Examples: in the morning, the tall building, to run
quickly. A clause contains a subject and a verb. An independent clause can
stand alone as a sentence. A dependent clause cannot stand alone and usually
begins with a subordinating conjunction or a relative pronoun. Example:
because it was raining.

===== Nouns and pronouns in detail =====

Most nouns form the plural by adding -s, as in book to books. Nouns ending in
-s, -x, -z, -ch, or -sh usually add -es, as in bus to buses, box to boxes, and
watch to watches. Nouns ending in a consonant plus -y change y to i and add
-es, as in city to cities. Many nouns ending in -f or -fe change to -ves, as
in leaf to leaves and knife to knives, but some simply add -s, as in roof to
roofs. Irregular plurals include man to men, woman to women, child to children,
mouse to mice, goose to geese, foot to feet, tooth to teeth, and person to
people.

Possessive nouns show ownership. For most singular nouns, add apostrophe s,
as in the dog's bone. For plural nouns ending in -s, add only an apostrophe,
as in the dogs' bones. For irregular plural nouns, add apostrophe s, as in the
children's toys. Do not use an apostrophe to form a simple plural.

Pronouns change form depending on their role in the sentence. Use subject
pronouns for subjects: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Use object pronouns
after verbs and prepositions: me, you, him, her, it, us, them. Example: She
gave the book to him. A common mistake is "between you and I"; the correct
form is "between you and me" because "between" is a preposition.

Use "who" for the subject of a clause and "whom" for the object. Example: Who
called you? To whom did you speak? In everyday conversation, "who" is often
used in place of "whom," but formal writing should follow the distinction.

Reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves and refer back to the subject.
Example: I taught myself to play. Do not use a reflexive pronoun when a plain
pronoun is correct. "Please contact myself" should be "Please contact me."

===== Verbs, tense, and aspect =====

Tense places an action in time. Aspect shows whether the action is complete,
ongoing, or repeated. English has three simple tenses, three progressive
tenses, three perfect tenses, and three perfect progressive tenses.

Simple present: I walk. She walks. Use it for habits, facts, and scheduled
events. Simple past: I walked. Use it for completed actions in the past.
Simple future: I will walk. Use it for actions that will happen later.

Present progressive: I am walking. Use it for actions happening now or around
now. Past progressive: I was walking. Use it for an ongoing action in the past,
often interrupted by another action. Future progressive: I will be walking.

Present perfect: I have walked. Use it for an action that happened at an
unspecified time before now, or for a state that began in the past and
continues. Past perfect: I had walked. Use it for an action completed before
another past action. Future perfect: I will have walked. Use it for an action
that will be completed before a future time.

Present perfect progressive: I have been walking. Past perfect progressive: I
had been walking. Future perfect progressive: I will have been walking.

Regular verbs form the past tense and past participle by adding -ed, as in
walk, walked, walked. Irregular verbs change in other ways, as in go, went,
gone; see, saw, seen; write, wrote, written; take, took, taken; and begin,
began, begun. Learn irregular verbs through examples and repetition.

The subject and verb must agree. A singular subject takes a singular verb, and
a plural subject takes a plural verb. Example: The cat runs. The cats run.
Words between the subject and verb do not change the agreement. Example: The
box of toys is heavy. Indefinite pronouns such as everyone, somebody, each,
and neither are usually singular. Example: Everyone is ready.

Collective nouns such as team, family, and group can take a singular or plural
verb depending on whether the group acts as one unit or as separate members.
In American English, singular agreement is more common. Example: The team is
winning. In British English, plural agreement is often used when the members
act individually.

===== Adjectives and adverbs =====

Adjectives describe nouns. Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives, or other
adverbs. Do not use an adjective where an adverb is needed. Example: She sings
beautifully, not She sings beautiful. Some verbs, called linking verbs, take an
adjective after them because the adjective describes the subject. Example:
The soup tastes good. The word "good" describes the soup, not the act of
tasting.

Comparative forms compare two things. Short adjectives usually add -er, as in
faster. Longer adjectives use "more," as in more comfortable. Superlative forms
compare three or more things. Short adjectives usually add -est, as in fastest.
Longer adjectives use "most," as in most comfortable. Never use both a
comparative ending and "more," as in "more faster." That is a double
comparative and is incorrect.

Some adjectives are absolute and should not normally be compared, such as
unique, perfect, and dead. In informal speech, people sometimes say "more
unique," but careful writers avoid it.

Order of adjectives in English is usually opinion, size, age, shape, color,
origin, material, and purpose. Example: a beautiful small old round blue
French wooden dining table. Native speakers rarely use so many adjectives at
once, but the order explains why "a big red ball" sounds natural and "a red big
ball" sounds strange.

===== Articles and determiners =====

Use "a" before a consonant sound and "an" before a vowel sound. The choice
depends on sound, not spelling. Example: a university, an hour, a European
country, an honest answer. Use "the" when the listener knows which specific
thing is meant, when the noun is unique, or when it has already been mentioned.
Example: I saw a dog. The dog was friendly.

Use no article for general plural nouns and uncountable nouns. Example: Cats
are independent. Water is essential. Use "the" for specific groups or
substances. Example: The cats in my neighborhood are noisy. The water in this
bottle is cold.

Determiners include articles, demonstratives, possessives, quantifiers, and
numbers. Examples: this, that, these, those, my, your, some, any, many, much,
few, little, several, every, each, either, neither, all, both, no. Choose the
determiner that matches whether the noun is countable or uncountable and
whether the meaning is specific or general.

===== Prepositions and common phrases =====

Prepositions can be tricky because usage is often idiomatic. Use "in" for
enclosed spaces, months, years, and long periods. Use "on" for surfaces, days,
and dates. Use "at" for precise times, points, and small locations. Example:
in the box, in July, on Monday, on the table, at noon, at the door.

Common preposition combinations include interested in, good at, afraid of,
proud of, responsible for, depend on, listen to, look at, wait for, arrive at,
arrive in, agree with, agree to, and different from. Some writers use
"different than" in American English, but "different from" is usually safer.

Do not end a sentence with a preposition if doing so creates an awkward
sentence, but ending with a preposition is often natural and correct. Example:
That is the book I was looking for. The rule against ending with a preposition
is not absolute.

===== Conjunctions and sentence combining =====

Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction that joins two independent
clauses. Example: I wanted to go, but it was raining. Do not use a comma if
the conjunction joins only words or phrases. Example: I bought bread and
cheese.

Use a semicolon to join two closely related independent clauses without a
conjunction. Example: The road was icy; we drove slowly. Use a semicolon
before a conjunctive adverb such as however, therefore, or meanwhile when it
joins two independent clauses. Example: The plan was risky; however, it
worked.

Use a colon to introduce a list, an explanation, or a quotation. Example: We
need three things: bread, milk, and eggs. Do not use a colon after a verb or
preposition unless the colon introduces a complete clause or a list.

Avoid comma splices. A comma splice occurs when two independent clauses are
joined only by a comma. Incorrect: I was tired, I went to bed. Correct: I was
tired, so I went to bed. Correct: I was tired; I went to bed. Correct: Because
I was tired, I went to bed.

===== Punctuation =====

A period ends a declarative sentence or an indirect question. A question mark
ends a direct question. An exclamation mark ends an exclamation and should be
used sparingly in formal writing.

A comma separates items in a list, separates introductory elements, sets off
nonessential information, and joins independent clauses with a coordinating
conjunction. The Oxford comma is the comma before the final item in a list of
three or more. Example: red, green, and blue. Many style guides recommend it
because it prevents ambiguity.

An apostrophe shows possession or marks a contraction. Examples: the book's
cover, don't, it's, they're. Do not use apostrophes to form plurals of ordinary
nouns. Use "its" for possession and "it's" for "it is" or "it has." Use "your"
for possession and "you're" for "you are." Use "their" for possession,
"there" for a place, and "they're" for "they are."

Quotation marks enclose direct speech or a quoted passage. In American English,
commas and periods usually go inside the closing quotation mark. In British
English, they often go outside unless they belong to the quotation. Use single
quotation marks for a quotation within a quotation.

A hyphen joins parts of a compound word or phrase, as in well-known or
twenty-one. A dash can set off a parenthetical idea or show a break in thought.
An ellipsis shows omitted words or a trailing thought. Use punctuation to make
meaning clear, not to decorate the page.

===== Capitalization =====

Capitalize the first word of every sentence, proper nouns, the pronoun I,
days of the week, months, holidays, languages, nationalities, geographic names,
and titles when they precede a name. Example: On Monday, Maria and I visited
London. Do not capitalize common nouns, seasons, or directions unless they are
part of a proper name. Example: We drove south in summer.

Capitalize the first word and all important words in a title. Small words such
as a, an, the, and, but, or, and prepositions are usually lowercase unless
they are the first or last word. Example: The Lord of the Rings.

===== Commonly confused words =====

Their means belonging to them. There means a place or a point. They're means
they are. Example: They're putting their books over there.

Your means belonging to you. You're means you are. Example: You're welcome to
bring your friend.

Its means belonging to it. It's means it is or it has. Example: It's raining,
and the dog wants its dinner.

Then refers to time or sequence. Than is used for comparison. Example: We ate
dinner, then we walked farther than before.

Affect is usually a verb meaning to influence. Effect is usually a noun
meaning a result. Example: The weather affects my mood. The effect was
immediate.

Fewer is used with countable nouns. Less is used with uncountable nouns.
Example: fewer apples, less water. In informal speech, "less" is often used
with numbers, as in "less than ten people," but "fewer than ten people" is more
precise.

Lie means to recline or rest. Lay means to put something down. Example: I lie
down to rest. I lay the book on the table. The past tense of lie is lay, and
the past tense of lay is laid. This is confusing even for native speakers.

Who's means who is or who has. Whose shows possession. Example: Who's coming
to dinner? Whose jacket is this?

Could have, should have, and would have are correct. "Could of," "should of,"
and "would of" are incorrect because "of" is not a verb.

Accept means to receive or agree to. Except means excluding. Example: I accept
your apology. Everyone came except Sam.

Advice is a noun. Advise is a verb. Example: She gave me good advice. I advise
you to rest.

Principal means main or a school leader. Principle means a rule or belief.
Example: The principal principle is honesty.

Stationary means not moving. Stationery means writing materials. Example: The
car was stationary. I bought stationery for school.

===== Spelling rules =====

The rule "i before e except after c" is useful but not perfect. Examples:
believe, receive, ceiling, science, weird, seize. Learn common exceptions as
whole words rather than relying only on the rhyme.

When adding a suffix to a word ending in silent e, drop the e if the suffix
begins with a vowel. Example: make to making, hope to hoping. Keep the e if the
suffix begins with a consonant. Example: hope to hopeful. Keep the e in words
such as changeable and noticeable to preserve the soft sound.

When adding a suffix to a one-syllable word ending in a consonant-vowel-
consonant pattern, double the final consonant if the suffix begins with a
vowel. Example: run to running, big to bigger, stop to stopped. Do not double
the consonant if the word has more than one syllable and the stress is not on
the final syllable. Example: visit to visiting.

For words ending in consonant plus y, change y to i before a suffix unless the
suffix begins with i. Example: happy to happiness, carry to carried, but carry
to carrying. For words ending in vowel plus y, keep the y. Example: play to
played.

===== Vocabulary building =====

A strong vocabulary helps you say exactly what you mean. Learn words in
context rather than as isolated lists. Read widely, notice how words combine,
and use a dictionary to check meaning, pronunciation, and usage. Record new
words with an example sentence and review them regularly.

Use precise verbs and nouns instead of vague ones. "Walk" is clear, but
"stroll," "march," "wander," and "hike" give different pictures. "Good" is
general, while "useful," "kind," "reliable," or "delicious" are more specific.

Distinguish between denotation and connotation. Denotation is the dictionary
meaning. Connotation is the feeling or association a word carries. "Cheap" and
"affordable" can describe a low price, but "cheap" may suggest poor quality.
"Childlike" and "childish" both relate to children, but one is positive and the
other is negative.

Avoid unnecessary repetition. Use pronouns, synonyms, and varied sentence
structure to keep writing interesting. Do not replace every word with a
synonym, however, because some synonyms have different shades of meaning.

===== Active and passive voice =====

In active voice, the subject performs the action. Example: The chef cooked the
meal. In passive voice, the subject receives the action. Example: The meal was
cooked by the chef. Active voice is usually clearer and more direct. Passive
voice is useful when the actor is unknown, unimportant, or should be
de-emphasized. Example: The bridge was built in 1900.

To form the passive, use a form of "be" plus the past participle. Example: The
letter was written. The letter has been written. The letter will be written.
Only transitive verbs, which take a direct object, can normally be passive.

===== Questions, negatives, and modals =====

Yes or no questions usually begin with a helping verb. Example: Do you like
tea? Have you eaten? Can she swim? Wh- questions begin with a question word:
who, what, when, where, why, which, whose, how. Example: Where did you go?

To make a negative sentence, use "not" after the first helping verb. If there
is no helping verb, use do, does, or did. Example: She is not ready. She does
not like coffee. She did not call.

Modal verbs include can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, and
would. They express ability, permission, possibility, obligation, advice, or
future time. Modal verbs do not add -s in the third person singular. Example:
She can swim, not She cans swim. After a modal verb, use the base form of the
main verb. Example: He must go, not He must goes.

===== Conditionals and reported speech =====

The first conditional describes a real future possibility. Example: If it
rains, we will stay inside. The second conditional describes an unreal or
hypothetical present situation. Example: If I had more time, I would travel.
The third conditional describes an unreal past situation. Example: If I had
studied, I would have passed.

Use "if" for conditions, "unless" for negative conditions, and "when" for
events that are expected. Example: Unless you hurry, you will be late.

In reported speech, tense often shifts back one step. Example: "I am tired,"
she said. She said that she was tired. Time words may also change. Example:
today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day, and here becomes there.
Use pronouns carefully so the meaning stays clear.

===== Writing clear paragraphs =====

A paragraph usually contains one main idea. Start with a topic sentence,
support it with details and examples, and end with a concluding sentence or a
transition. Keep sentences focused. If a sentence contains several unrelated
ideas, split it.

Use transitions to show relationships between ideas: however, therefore, for
example, in addition, meanwhile, as a result, on the other hand, first, next,
finally. Transitions should guide the reader, not decorate the text.

Prefer the active voice, concrete nouns, and strong verbs. Cut unnecessary
words. "Due to the fact that" can become "because." "At this point in time" can
become "now." "In order to" can often become "to." Clear writing is usually
shorter than vague writing.

===== Formal and informal English =====

Informal English is common in conversation, personal messages, and some social
media. It includes contractions, slang, sentence fragments, and casual
punctuation. Formal English is common in academic writing, business documents,
and official communication. It usually avoids slang, uses complete sentences,
and follows standard punctuation.

Choose the register that fits the audience and purpose. A message to a friend
can be relaxed. A job application should be polished. Neither register is
inherently better; each is appropriate in its own setting.

===== Practice examples =====

Incorrect: Me and him went to the store. Correct: He and I went to the store.
The subject form is needed, and the pronoun I comes after the other person.

Incorrect: The report was wrote by the intern. Correct: The report was written
by the intern. The passive voice uses the past participle.

Incorrect: Each of the students have a book. Correct: Each of the students has
a book. "Each" is singular.

Incorrect: She is more taller than her sister. Correct: She is taller than her
sister. Do not combine more with an -er ending.

Incorrect: Their going to the beach with there friends. Correct: They're going
to the beach with their friends.

Incorrect: I have went to that restaurant before. Correct: I have gone to that
restaurant before. Use the past participle with have.

Incorrect: Between you and I, the plan is risky. Correct: Between you and me,
the plan is risky. A preposition takes an object pronoun.

Incorrect: The dog wagged it's tail. Correct: The dog wagged its tail. "Its"
shows possession.

Incorrect: He don't know the answer. Correct: He doesn't know the answer.
Third person singular takes "does not."

Incorrect: We discussed about the problem. Correct: We discussed the problem.
"Discuss" does not need "about."

===== A final checklist =====

Read the sentence aloud. Check that the subject and verb agree. Check that
pronouns refer clearly to the right noun. Check tense consistency. Check
punctuation, especially commas and apostrophes. Check commonly confused words.
Make sure each paragraph has one main idea. Cut words that do not add meaning.

Grammar is a tool for clarity. Rules matter, but meaning matters more. When a
rule and clarity conflict, choose the version that helps the reader understand
you. Revise, read your work again, and ask whether each sentence says exactly
what you intended.

user: how do i get stone
ultron: Stone makes up the majority of the solid blocks generated in the Overworld above Y=0. From Y=8 downward, stone gradually transitions into deepslate, until it is completely replaced by deepslate at and below Y=0. When chunks generate, stone can be found under 1-5 layers of grass blocks, dirt, gravel, clay, coarse dirt, podzol, mycelium, sand, sandstone, red sand, red sandstone, or terracotta, depending on the biome.

A player can prevent this, and place two small chests side by side, by sneaking while placing the second chest in Java Edition, pushing a chest into place with a piston in Bedrock Edition, or placing the second chest facing a different direction from the first chest.

user: what does command block do
ultron: A command block can execute commands when activated by redstone power. It always has permissions of level 2‌[Java Edition only]/level 1‌[Bedrock Edition only], so it can be used to allow a specific use of a command by players who can't use that command in general (for example, allowing anyone to obtain a specific item with /give without allowing everyone to /give themselves whatever they want). A command block has an orientation that determines the chain command block to activate, and the blocks to be checked to see if a command block in "Conditional" mode executes.

user: how do i get iron ore
ultron: Iron ore generates in three batches. The first batch attempts to generate 90 times per chunk in blobs of 0–13‌[JE only] or 0–16‌[BE only], from levels 80 to 384, being most common around level 232 and becoming less common toward either end of the range. The second batch attempts to generate 10 times per chunk in blobs of 0–13‌[JE only] or 0–16‌[BE only], from levels −24 to 56, being most common around level 16 and becoming less common toward either end of the range.

user: what is redstone dust
ultron: Redstone dust (or simply redstone) is a mineral used in crafting, brewing, and trimming, as well as being used as a placeable wire. Redstone wire is a non-solid block that can transmit a redstone power signal up to 15 blocks in distance; signal strengths below 15 have reduced distance. Redstone wire can power blocks it is placed on or pointing at.

user: what is anvil mechanics
ultron: This page explains the mechanics of the anvil. The anvil is primarily used in its inventory to combine tools, weapons, and armor with other items of the same type or with an enchanted book at the cost of experience without the stripping of enchantments, or to rename any item. The item on the left side of an anvil operation is known as the target, and any item on the right is known as the sacrifice.

user: what is status effect
ultron: An effect (also known as a mob effect or status effect) is a condition that affects an entity, either negatively, positively, or neutrally. Effects usually can be inflicted in various ways throughout the game, including potions, some food items, being shot by certain arrows, being in the range of active beacons and conduits, noxious gas from potent sulfur, and being attacked by certain mobs. The /effect command allows players to inflict effects upon themselves and other entities with different levels of these effects.

ultron: By using the F3 + B shortcut, the dragon's bounding box appears.‌[Java Edition only] However, it cannot be damaged at just any spot in this large volume: eight green sub-hitboxes are also shown, which indicate the locations where the dragon can take damage: the tail (three hitboxes), body, head, neck, and right and left wings. Name tags cannot be used on an ender dragon, because it is not possible to interact directly with it, only with its parts (green hitboxes), which are not living entities. An ender dragon killed by /kill‌[Java Edition only] or from damage belonging to the type self_destruct, and not spawned from the player‌[Bedrock Edition only], skips its death animation and the exit portal immediately opens; in Bedrock Edition, if the dragon was killed by /kill it remains in the same place and plays its death animation there instead of flying to the exit portal.

They require only grass blocks with air above (clear of any plants such as flowers or short grass), and can generate regardless whether that grass block has a layer of snow cover. Practically speaking, this means that the occurrence of pumpkins in stony or sandy biomes, or in grassy biomes with few clear grass blocks, is comparatively rare.

user: what is redstone circuit
ultron: A redstone circuit is a build that primarily focuses on dealing with logic and redstone signals using redstone. Circuits can be used to transmit redstone signals, perform operations with logic gates, store information, shorten and lengthen redstone signals, make redstone clocks, and more. A useful distinction can be made between a circuit performing operations on signals (generating, modifying, combining, etc.), and a mechanism using the environment (moving blocks, opening doors, changing the light level, producing sound, etc).

user: what does observer do
ultron: An observer is placed directionally. When placed, the observing face (the side with the "eyes") always faces away from the player, detecting most changes in the block directly in front of it. The output side (featuring a red dot) faces toward the player and emits a redstone pulse whenever the observing face detects a change.

user: what does resource pack do
ultron: Each resource pack is either a directory or a ZIP archive (with .zip extension). Resource packs can be added by placing them in the resourcepacks directory within .minecraft, or by dragging and dropping onto the "Select Resource Packs" screen, which copies them there automatically. Resource packs present in the directory can then be managed from the options, where they can be moved between "Available" (disabled) and "Selected" (enabled), and reordered.

user: what does big dripleaf do
ultron: Big dripleaves consist of any number of non-solid stem blocks atop of each other and a single leaf as the uppermost block, which can be stood on by any entity like a normal block for 10 game ticks (0.5 seconds). After this time, it tilts down, becoming lower than a block and giving a player warning that it is about to collapse. After a 10 more game ticks, it tilts down and becomes temporarily non-solid.

user: what is calibrated sculk sensor
ultron: A calibrated sculk sensor is a craftable type of sculk sensor that functions similarly, but detects vibrations more often and from further away. Its amethyst-covered input side can be powered to make the sensor only detect vibrations from specific sources, depending on the signal strength used. Placing an amethyst block next to a calibrated sculk sensor allows it to "relay" detected vibrations to sculk sensors or other calibrated sculk sensors.

user: what does calibrated sculk sensor do
ultron: When a calibrated sculk sensor detects a vibration, it is activated and emits redstone signal in every direction (including top and bottom), except the side with the amethyst stripe. The redstone signal emitted from the bottom will strongly power the block below the sensor, whereas in all other directions (excluding the side with the amethyst stripe) it is as though the sensor itself is the strongly powered block.

user: what does copper chest do
ultron: A copper chest placed adjacent to another copper chest joins to create a large copper chest. Two adjacent copper chests merge into a large copper chest even if the two chests have different oxidization levels or waxed states; in such cases, the resulting large chest takes the oxidization level of the least oxidized half, and is unwaxed if one of the two halves is unwaxed. A player can prevent the formation of a large chest, and place two small copper chests side by side, by sneaking while placing the second chest in Java Edition, pushing a copper chest into place with a piston in Bedrock Edition, or placing the second chest facing a different direction from the first chest.

user: what is bedrock edition
ultron: In Bedrock Edition, dyes cannot be applied to armor directly and are applied to cauldron water instead. When a dye is used on dyed cauldron water, the resulting color is the average of the color in the cauldron and the applied color in sRGB, with each component ranging from 0 (no intensity) to 1 (maximum intensity).

user: what is falling
ultron: A mace does a smash attack when it is used after the player has fallen 1.5 blocks or more, regardless of the mace's current attack cooldown progress. user: what is redstone circuits
ultron: A redstone circuit is a build that primarily focuses on dealing with logic and redstone signals using redstone. Circuits can be used to transmit redstone signals, perform operations with logic gates, store information, shorten and lengthen redstone signals, make redstone clocks, and more. A useful distinction can be made between a circuit performing operations on signals (generating, modifying, combining, etc.), and a mechanism using the environment (moving blocks, opening doors, changing the light level, producing sound, etc).

user: how do i get golden chest
ultron: Golden chests are not a separate block and thus cannot be obtained with the command /give or through the Creative inventory. To create a golden chest without minecraft:midas_touch activated, the player can use the /setblock command with a regular or trapped chest and the tag "gold": /setblock ~ ~ ~ minecraft:chest{gold:1b}, or /setblock ~ ~ ~ minecraft:trapped_chest{gold:1b}. Opening a large chest with midas_touch changes the chest visually, but the texture is glitched.

user: what is redstone components
ultron: Redstone components are the blocks used to build redstone circuits. Redstone components include power source components (such as redstone torches, buttons, and pressure plates), transmission components (such as redstone dust and redstone repeaters), and mechanism components (such as pistons, doors, and redstone lamps). This article assumes familiarity with the basics of redstone structures.

user: what does breach do
ultron: Breach reduces the effectiveness of the target's armor points and armor toughness by 15% per level. Specifically, Breach deals damage as though the enemy's damage reduction from armor was 15 percentage points lower per level. For example, if the enemy's armor reduces damage by 50%, and they are hit with a mace with Breach I, their armor reduces the damage by 50% - 15% = 35%.

user: what does channeling do
ultron: Channeling summons a lightning bolt when an entity or lightning rod is hit by a thrown trident, if there is currently a thunderstorm occurring, including in dry biomes. This applies to most entities that the trident can collide with: mobs, players, armor stands, boats, minecarts, end crystals, item frames, paintings, leash knots, and even shulker bullets. It does not apply to ghast fireballs and wind charges, and to entities that the trident can't collide with (small fireballs, arrows, experience orbs, thrown item entities, primed TNT, falling blocks, wither projectiles, and so on).
